how-music-works.wrapped_text:
How Music Works
How does a note on paper become a
sound, and how does a listener
hear it? Music is sound arranged
in time. Its basic building block
is the note: one distinct sound
with a pitch, a length and a
loudness. The word also names the
symbol that writes the sound on
paper ([Musical note](https://en.w
ikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_note)).
Pitch is how high or low a
listener hears a sound.

A note travels along a path. A
composer writes it on a score. A
player reads the score and presses
a key, bows a string or sings. The
instrument makes the air vibrate,
and the vibration reaches the ear
of a listener, who hears a pitch
again. This map follows one note
along that path, in five parts:

- [Sound and
Pitch](#sound-and-pitch): the
sound of one note is a pressure
wave that repeats. The wave is a
sum of sine waves at whole
multiples of one frequency, and
the listener hears that frequency
as the pitch.
- [The Pitch
System](#pitch-system): Western
music uses a fixed grid of
pitches. The grid splits each
octave, which is a doubling of
frequency, into 12 equal steps
called semitones.
- [The Piano
Keyboard](#piano-keyboard): the
piano has one key for each of 88
pitches of the grid, from 27.5 Hz
to 4,186 Hz.
- [Sheet Music](#sheet-music): a
score works like a plot of pitch
against time. The height of a note
on the staff gives its key, and
the shape of the note gives its
length.
- [Hearing Pitch](#hearing-pitch):
the inner ear splits sound into
frequency bands. Many musicians
can hear the interval between two
notes, but few people can name a
single note.

Musicians also say tone. A musical
tone is a steady periodic sound
with a length, a pitch, a loudness
and a timbre ([Musical tone](https
://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_t
one)). The word has two more
meanings in music. A whole tone is
a step of two semitones, and tone
color is another name for
[Timbre](#timbre), the sound
quality that tells a piano from a
violin.

harmonics.wrapped_text:
A Note Is a Sum of Harmonics
The signal of a sustained note from a string,
a wind instrument or a voice repeats with a
period T. As a periodic signal, it is a
Fourier series: a sum of sine waves at the
fundamental frequency f0 = 1/T and at the
whole multiples 2·f0, 3·f0, 4·f0 and so on.
Each sine wave has its own amplitude and phase
([Musical tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Musical_tone)). Musicians call these sine
waves harmonics, and the list of them is the
[harmonic series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wik
i/Harmonic_series_%28music%29). The
fundamental is the first harmonic. The tuning
note of an orchestra, A4, is a combination of
440 Hz, 880 Hz, 1,320 Hz, 1,760 Hz and higher
multiples ([Timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/w
iki/Timbre)).

A real note is more than this steady part. Its
start, the attack, has transients that do not
repeat, and its envelope and pitch can change
while it sounds ([Musical tone](https://en.wik
ipedia.org/wiki/Musical_tone)).

The physics of the instrument makes the
multiples. A string is fixed at both ends, so
it vibrates only in modes that fit a whole
number of half waves along its length. Mode n
has the frequency n·f0, and the string
vibrates in many modes at the same time. The
air column of a wind instrument works the same
way ([harmonic series](https://en.wikipedia.or
g/wiki/Harmonic_series_%28music%29)). In a
piano, a bridge passes the vibration of the
strings to the soundboard, which couples it to
the air ([Piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki
/Piano)).

Three words name the parts of the spectrum. A
partial is any sine component. A harmonic is a
partial at a whole multiple of f0. An overtone
is any partial above the lowest one. A pure
tone is a single sine wave. A synthesizer can
make one, and some flutes and ocarinas come
close ([harmonic series](https://en.wikipedia.
org/wiki/Harmonic_series_%28music%29)).

pitch.wrapped_text:
Pitch Follows the Period
Pitch is a perception of the listener, and
frequency is a physical quantity that an
instrument measures. The American National
Standards Institute defines pitch as the
attribute of sound that lets a listener order
sounds from low to high ([Pitch](https://en.wi
kipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_%28music%29)). For a
periodic or nearly periodic sound, the pitch
is very close to the repetition rate 1/T,
which is f0.

The ear finds the period even when the f0
component is absent. A sound made of only
1,000 Hz and 1,200 Hz repeats every 5 ms. A
listener can hear a pitch of 200 Hz in it, in
addition to the two tones ([Pitch](https://en.
wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_%28music%29)). This
effect is the missing fundamental. The heard
pitch is usually the greatest common divisor
of the frequencies that are present. A
telephone passes little sound below 300 Hz,
but a male voice with f0 near 150 Hz keeps its
pitch on the phone. The brain computes the
fundamental from the overtones ([Missing funda
mental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missing_
fundamental)).

timbre.wrapped_text:
Timbre Is the Shape of the Spectrum
Timbre, also called tone color, makes a guitar
and a piano sound different when they play the
same note at the same loudness. The Acoustical
Society of America defines it as the attribute
that lets a listener judge two sounds as
different when they have the same loudness and
pitch ([Timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Timbre)). Two physical properties set it:

- The spectrum: the relative amplitudes of the
harmonics. Every instrument of an orchestra
plays the A4 tuning note at 440 Hz, 880 Hz,
1,320 Hz and so on, and each instrument has
its own balance of these amplitudes ([Timbre](
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre)).
- The envelope: the change of amplitude over
time. It is often described in four phases:
attack, decay, sustain and release (ADSR). A
piano note has a loud attack that fades fast,
followed by a soft sustain ([Piano acoustics](
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_acoustics)
).

The player and the maker also shape the
spectrum. A hard piano hammer makes loud, very
high harmonics, so piano hammers have a felt
cover that is soft enough to avoid them ([Pian
o](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano)).
Helmholtz stated that timbre depends on the
amplitudes of the partials and not on their
phases. Research since then shows that the ear
acts as a simple Fourier analyzer only under
restricted conditions ([Ohm's acoustic law](ht
tps://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohm%27s_acoustic_l
aw)).

inharmonicity.wrapped_text:
Real Partials Run Sharp
The whole-number rule is exact for an ideal
string, which bends with no resistance. A real
piano string is stiff. Stiffness makes the
string dispersive: the wave speed rises with
frequency, so the upper partials sit a little
above n·f0. This deviation is inharmonicity ([
Inharmonicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I
nharmonicity)). In a piano, it grows toward
both ends of the keyboard. A tuner sets each
higher note so that its fundamental matches a
sharp overtone of a lower note. As a result,
the octaves of a tuned piano are slightly
wider than 2:1. The Railsback curve shows how
far each note sits from the grid formula, in
cents ([Piano acoustics](https://en.wikipedia.
org/wiki/Piano_acoustics)).

A bowed string, or an air column driven by a
reed or by the lips, locks its partials to
exact whole multiples. This effect is
mode-locking. A struck or plucked string
vibrates freely and keeps its inharmonicity ([
Inharmonicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I
nharmonicity)). Tubular bells, timpani and
marimbas have mostly inharmonic partials, but
a few strong partials still give the ear a
pitch. Cymbals make spectra rich in inharmonic
partials, and they can give no sense of a
particular pitch ([harmonic series](https://en
.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_series_%28music%2
9)).

pitch-system.wrapped_text:
The Pitch System
A pitch system is the set of
pitches that a music tradition
uses. The distance between two
pitches is an interval. Its exact
size is the ratio of the two
frequencies. Musicians name an
interval by counting the letter
names that it spans, both ends
included: from B up to D is a
third, because B, C and D are
three letters ([Interval](https://
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_%28
music%29)).

Western music, the music tradition
that grew in Europe, builds its
pitch system in two steps. First,
it gives notes an octave apart the
same name. Next, it splits every
octave into 12 equal steps. The
steps are equal as frequency
ratios, so the grid is uniform on
a logarithmic frequency axis.

octave.wrapped_text:
Octave
An octave is the interval between a pitch and
the pitch with twice its frequency. A4 is 440
Hz, A5 is 880 Hz and A3 is 220 Hz ([Octave](ht
tps://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave)). The
octave is also the step from the first
harmonic to the second. Western notation gives
notes an octave apart the same letter name.
Music theory calls all pitches with one name,
in every octave, a pitch class. The pitch
class C holds C1, C2, C3 and every other C
([Pitch class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P
itch_class)).

twelve-semitones.wrapped_text:
Twelve Semitones
Western music splits each octave into 12 equal
frequency ratios. This tuning is twelve-tone
equal temperament. One step is a semitone,
with the ratio 2^(1/12), about 1.059463.
Twelve semitones multiply to 2, which is one
octave ([Piano key frequencies](https://en.wik
ipedia.org/wiki/Piano_key_frequencies)). The
standard ISO 16 sets A4 to 440 Hz ([A440](http
s://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A440_%28pitch_standa
rd%29)). Every other pitch follows from it:
the pitch n semitones above A4 has the
frequency 440 × 2^(n/12) Hz, and a negative n
gives a pitch below A4.

Musicians measure intervals in cents, a
logarithmic unit. A semitone is 100 cents and
an octave is 1,200 cents. The interval from f1
up to f2 is 1200 × log2(f2/f1) cents ([Cent](h
ttps://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cent_%28music%29)
).

The equal steps come close to the whole-number
ratios between neighboring harmonics. The
fifths and fourths of the grid are almost
exact, and its thirds are further away ([Equal
temperament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equ
al_temperament), [Interval](https://en.wikiped
ia.org/wiki/Interval_%28music%29)):

| Ratio | Pure interval | Nearest grid
interval |
|---|---|---|
| 3:2, harmonic 2 to harmonic 3 | Fifth:
701.96 cents | 7 semitones: 700 cents |
| 4:3, harmonic 3 to harmonic 4 | Fourth:
498.04 cents | 5 semitones: 500 cents |
| 5:4, harmonic 4 to harmonic 5 | Major third:
386.31 cents | 4 semitones: 400 cents |

The 14-cent gap of the major third is large
enough to hear ([Cent](https://en.wikipedia.or
g/wiki/Cent_%28music%29)). The harmonics of
one note also land near grid pitches. For A4,
the harmonic at 1,320 Hz is 2 cents above E6,
the one at 2,200 Hz is 14 cents below C♯7, and
the one at 3,080 Hz is 31 cents below G7.
About the Numbers shows the calculation.

other-pitch-grids.wrapped_text:
Other Pitch Grids
Other music traditions use pitches between the
keys of the Western grid. An interval smaller
than a semitone is a microtone ([Microtonality
](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microtonality)
). Four examples:

- Persian classical music lowers a note by
about a quarter tone with the koron sign, and
raises it by a quarter tone with the sori
sign. A quarter tone is half a semitone, 50
cents ([Quarter tone](https://en.wikipedia.org
/wiki/Quarter_tone)). The Iranian musician
Alinaghi Vaziri set the standard use of the
koron sign in the early 20th century ([Koron](
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koron_%28music%2
9)).
- Arabic maqam music builds its scales from
seconds of four sizes. One of them, the
neutral second, lies between the minor second
of one semitone and the major second of two
semitones ([Arabic maqam](https://en.wikipedia
.org/wiki/Arabic_maqam)).
- Indian music theory names 22 shrutis in an
octave. A shruti is the smallest step of
pitch, and the 7 swaras, the notes of a scale,
are chosen from them ([Shruti](https://en.wiki
pedia.org/wiki/Shruti_%28music%29)).
- Indonesian gamelan music uses two tunings:
slendro, with five notes per octave, and
pelog, with seven. The exact pitches change
from one ensemble to another ([Slendro](https:
//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slendro),
[Pelog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelog)).

instruments-and-the-grid.wrapped_text:
Instruments and the Grid
Instruments differ in the pitches that they
can make. They fall into three kinds:

- Fixed pitch: each key, string, pipe or bar
sounds one set pitch. The piano, the harp and
the xylophone are examples, and a slide across
one of them is a run of separate steps ([Gliss
ando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glissando)
). The piano covers 27.5 Hz to 4,186 Hz. A
large pipe organ goes lower: some organs have
a pipe for C−1, which is 8 Hz and below the
range of hearing ([Range](https://en.wikipedia
.org/wiki/Range_%28music%29)).
- Continuous pitch: the player can set the
frequency anywhere in a range. Examples are
the violin, viola, cello and double bass,
which have no frets, the trombone, the
theremin and the human voice ([Glissando](http
s://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glissando)). The
theremin is an electronic instrument. Its tone
is the difference frequency of two
radio-frequency oscillators, and the player
detunes one of them with a hand near an
antenna ([Theremin](https://en.wikipedia.org/w
iki/Theremin)).
- No pitch: unpitched percussion, such as the
snare drum, makes noise-like or inharmonic
sound with no clear fundamental. It keeps the
rhythm and adds accents ([Unpitched percussion
instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unpi
tched_percussion_instrument)).

Players of continuous-pitch instruments use
pitches between the grid steps. Vibrato is a
periodic frequency modulation of a note. A
solo singer's vibrato usually swings less than
100 cents to each side of the note ([Vibrato](
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibrato)). These
players can also tune an interval to an exact
whole-number ratio, such as 5:4 for a major
third. Such pure intervals are just intonation
([Just intonation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wi
ki/Just_intonation)).

The grid holds 120 equal-tempered notes from
16 Hz to 16,000 Hz, and a listener can tell
about 1,400 pitch steps apart over the range
of hearing ([Pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/w
iki/Pitch_%28music%29)). The range of an
instrument is the span from its lowest to its
highest pitch ([Range](https://en.wikipedia.or
g/wiki/Range_%28music%29)). The concert flute,
for example, has a higher and narrower range
than the piano, and flute players call C4 "low
C" ([C (musical note)](https://en.wikipedia.or
g/wiki/C_%28musical_note%29)).

Instruments and the Grid
Instruments differ in the pitches that they can make. They fall into three kinds:

- Fixed pitch: each key, string, pipe or bar sounds one set pitch. The piano, the harp and the xylophone are examples, and a slide across one of them is a run of separate steps ([Glissando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glissando)). The piano covers 27.5 Hz to 4,186 Hz. A large pipe organ goes lower: some organs have a pipe for C−1, which is 8 Hz and below the range of hearing ([Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Range_%28music%29)).
- Continuous pitch: the player can set the frequency anywhere in a range. Examples are the violin, viola, cello and double bass, which have no frets, the trombone, the theremin and the human voice ([Glissando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glissando)). The theremin is an electronic instrument. Its tone is the difference frequency of two radio-frequency oscillators, and the player detunes one of them with a hand near an antenna ([Theremin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theremin)).
- No pitch: unpitched percussion, such as the snare drum, makes noise-like or inharmonic sound with no clear fundamental. It keeps the rhythm and adds accents ([Unpitched percussion instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unpitched_percussion_instrument)).

Players of continuous-pitch instruments use pitches between the grid steps. Vibrato is a periodic frequency modulation of a note. A solo singer's vibrato usually swings less than 100 cents to each side of the note ([Vibrato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibrato)). These players can also tune an interval to an exact whole-number ratio, such as 5:4 for a major third. Such pure intervals are just intonation ([Just intonation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_intonation)).

The grid holds 120 equal-tempered notes from 16 Hz to 16,000 Hz, and a listener can tell about 1,400 pitch steps apart over the range of hearing ([Pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_%28music%29)). The range of an instrument is the span from its lowest to its highest pitch ([Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Range_%28music%29)). The concert flute, for example, has a higher and narrower range than the piano, and flute players call C4 "low C" ([C (musical note)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_%28musical_note%29)).

frequency.

key-press.wrapped_text:
What a Key Press Does
Pressing a key makes a felt-covered hammer
strike the strings of that note and fall back
at once. A bass note has one string, a tenor
note two and a treble note three. A bridge
passes the vibration to the soundboard, which
couples it to the air. A harder press makes
the hammer hit harder and the note louder.
When the key comes up, a damper stops the
strings ([Piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki
/Piano)).

The pianist therefore controls three things
for each note: which key, how hard, and how
long the key stays down. These match the
pitch, the loudness and the length that the
score asks for. MIDI records a played note in
the same terms. A note-on message carries the
note number and a velocity, which tells how
hard the key was struck, and a later note-off
message ends the note
([MIDI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIDI)).

The sustain pedal is the right pedal. It lifts
all dampers, so the notes keep sounding after
the keys come up ([Piano](https://en.wikipedia
.org/wiki/Piano)).

Sheet Music
Sheet music, or a score, writes
music as symbols on a staff. The
staff works like a graph of pitch
against time: a higher note sits
higher, and the notes are played
from left to right. The horizontal
position gives the time only
roughly. The shape of each note
and the tempo give the exact
timing ([Staff](https://en.wikiped
ia.org/wiki/Staff_%28music%29)).
Notes stacked at the same
horizontal place sound together as
a chord, which is the sound of two
or more notes at the same time ([C
hord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wik
i/Chord_%28music%29)).

page shows three more things. Its
note value gives its length
relative to the other notes. Its
dynamics tell how loud to play it.
Its articulation tells how to
shape its attack and its end
([Musical note](https://en.wikiped
ia.org/wiki/Musical_note)). Rests
mark silences, and the tempo sets
the speed of the beat. The nodes
below explain each part:

- Notes on the Staff: the pitch.
- Note Lengths and Rests: the
length of each note and of each
silence.

notes-on-the-staff.wrapped_text:
Notes on the Staff
A staff is five horizontal lines with four
spaces between them. A note head sits on a
line or in a space. When no sharp or flat
applies, each step from a line to the next
space up is one white key up ([Staff](https://
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staff_%28music%29),
[Musical keyboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wi
ki/Musical_keyboard)). A clef at the left end
of the staff fixes one line to one note, and
the other positions follow from that line
([Clef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clef)):

- The treble clef 𝄞, or G clef, puts G4 on the
second line from the bottom. The curl of the
clef wraps around that line.
- The bass clef 𝄢, or F clef, puts F3 on the
fourth line from the bottom. The two dots of
the clef sit above and below that line.

The clef signs grew out of the letters G and
F, which scribes once wrote on the reference
line
([Clef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clef)).

Piano music uses the grand staff: two staves
joined by a brace, with a treble staff above
and a bass staff below. The right hand
normally plays the upper staff, and the left
hand plays the lower staff. Middle C sits
between the two staves on a short extra line,
a ledger line. Ledger lines extend a staff for
notes above or below it ([Staff](https://en.wi
kipedia.org/wiki/Staff_%28music%29), [Ledger l
ine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ledger_line
)).

The picture puts each line and space of the
grand staff above its white key. Printed music
leaves a wider gap between the two staves. The
picture keeps every step the same height, so
middle C sits exactly halfway between the
staves.



Learners often memorize the line and space
names with phrases
([Clef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clef)):

| Staff | Lines, bottom to top | Spaces,
bottom to top |
|---|---|---|
| Treble | E4 G4 B4 D5 F5: Every Good Boy Does
Fine | F4 A4 C5 E5: FACE |
| Bass | G2 B2 D3 F3 A3: Good Boys Do Fine
Always | A2 C3 E3 G3: All Cows Eat Grass |

accidentals.wrapped_text:
Sharps, Flats and Key Signature
An accidental is a sign in front of a note
that moves the note by a semitone ([Accidental
](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accidental_%28
music%29)):

- A sharp (♯) raises the note one semitone:
play the next key to the right.
- A flat (♭) lowers the note one semitone:
play the next key to the left.
- A natural (♮) cancels a sharp or a flat.

An accidental also applies to later notes on
the same line or space, up to the next bar
line. A bar line is the vertical line that
ends a bar of music, and Beat, Bar and Tempo
explains bars. A key signature is a group of
sharps or flats right after the clef. It
applies to every note with that letter, in
every octave, until the piece ends or a new
key signature appears. For example, a flat in
the top space of the treble staff turns every
E into E♭, including E4 on the bottom line
([Key signature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki
/Key_signature)).

Note Lengths and Rests
The shape of a note gives its length relative
to the other notes. The note head, the stem
and the flags or beams show the value. Each
value lasts half as long as the value before
it ([Note value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki
/Note_value)). Eighth notes and shorter notes
are usually joined in groups by beams.
American and British books use different names
for the values, as the picture shows.



A rest is a silence of a set length. Each note
value has a matching rest with its own sign,
for example a quarter rest for the silence of
one quarter note ([Rest](https://en.wikipedia.
org/wiki/Rest_%28music%29)). A dot after a
note makes it 1.5 times as long. A tie is a
curved line between two notes of the same
pitch. It joins them into one note that lasts
as long as both together ([Dotted note](https:
//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dotted_note), [Tie](ht
tps://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tie_%28music%29)).

beat-bar-tempo.wrapped_text:
Beat, Bar and Tempo
Players count time in beats. The time
signature, two stacked numbers after the clef,
sets the beat and groups the beats into bars,
which are also called measures. The lower
number names the note value that gets one
beat: 2 is a half note, 4 a quarter note and 8
an eighth note. The upper number is the count
of beats in one bar. In 4/4 time, one bar
holds four quarter notes. The most common time
signatures are 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 ([Time signatu
re](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_signatu
re)). Vertical bar lines separate the bars ([B
ar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_%28music
%29)).

The tempo is the speed of the beat in beats
per minute (BPM). A metronome mark such as ♩ =
120 asks for 120 quarter notes per minute.
Many scores use an Italian word instead of a
number, or with it. The words give only rough
speeds, and the ranges below are for 4/4 time 
([Tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo))
:

- Largo: slow and broad, about 40 to 66 BPM.
- Andante: at a walking pace, about 56 to 108
BPM.
- Allegro: fast and bright, about 120 to 156
BPM.
- Presto: very fast, about 168 to 200 BPM.

A note of b beats lasts b × 60 / BPM seconds.
At ♩ = 120, one beat lasts 60 / 120 = 0.5 s:

| Symbol | Beats in 4/4 time | Seconds at ♩ =
120 |
|---|---|---|
| Whole note or whole rest | 4 | 2.0 |
| Half note or half rest | 2 | 1.0 |
| Dotted quarter note | 1.5 | 0.75 |
| Quarter note or quarter rest | 1 | 0.5 |
| Eighth note or eighth rest | 0.5 | 0.25 |

One bar of 4/4 time at this tempo lasts 2.0 s.

loudness-and-touch.wrapped_text:
Loudness and Touch
Dynamics marks give the loudness. They are
short forms of Italian words: p, for piano,
means soft, and f, for forte, means loud. The
scale runs pp, p, mp, mf, f and ff, from very
soft to very loud. The marks are relative and
set no level in decibels. A crescendo asks for
a gradual rise in loudness, and a decrescendo
asks for a gradual fall. Scores often draw
them as hairpins that span several notes: an
opening < for a crescendo and a closing > for
a decrescendo ([Dynamics](https://en.wikipedia
.org/wiki/Dynamics_%28music%29)). On the
piano, a harder press of the key gives a
louder note.

Articulation marks tell how a note starts, how
long it really sounds and how it joins the
next note ([Articulation](https://en.wikipedia
.org/wiki/Articulation_%28music%29)):

- Staccato: a dot above or below the note asks
for a short note with a silence after it ([Sta
ccato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staccato)
).
- Legato: a slur, a curved line over or under
notes of different pitches, asks for notes
without gaps between them. A slur looks like a
tie, but a tie joins notes of the same pitch (
[Slur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slur_%28m
usic%29), [Tie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Tie_%28music%29)).
- Accent: a small horizontal wedge > on one
note asks for a stressed start that then fades
quickly ([Accent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wik
i/Accent_%28music%29)). A hairpin is longer
and spans several notes.

Piano scores also show where to use the
sustain pedal ([Piano pedals](https://en.wikip
edia.org/wiki/Piano_pedals)).

read-and-play.wrapped_text:
Reading and Playing a Piece
A beginner can play a piece in this order:

1. Find the clefs. The right hand plays the
treble staff, and the left hand plays the bass
staff.
2. Read the key signature. Remember which
letters are sharp or flat in the whole piece.
3. Read the time signature and the tempo.
Count one bar of beats aloud at the tempo
before you start.
4. For each note, find its line or space, name
it from the clef, and find its key. Apply the
key signature and any accidental earlier in
the bar.
5. Press the key on its beat and hold it for

The Ear Splits Sound by Frequency
Sound reaches the cochlea, a spiral tube in
the inner ear that is filled with fluid. The
basilar membrane runs along the tube. Each
part of the membrane, together with the fluid
around it, acts like a mass-spring resonator.
Near the entrance of the tube, at the base,
the membrane is stiff and light and responds
to high frequencies. At the far end, the apex,
it is floppy and heavy and responds to low
frequencies. A sine tone therefore makes one
place vibrate most. This map from frequency to
place is called tonotopy ([Basilar membrane](h
ttps://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilar_membrane)
). About 3,500 inner hair cells along the
membrane turn its motion into nerve signals
([Hair cell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hai
r_cell)). Hearing research models each place
as a band-pass filter, the auditory filter,
and calls its bandwidth the critical band
([Critical band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki
/Critical_band)).

The ear hears from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz,
and the upper limit falls with age ([Hearing r
ange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearing_ra
nge)). Above 1,000 Hz, a listener notices a
change of about 0.6% in a sine tone, which is
about 10 cents. Below 500 Hz, the smallest
change that a listener notices is about 3 Hz
for a sine tone and 1 Hz for a tone with
harmonics ([Pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wi
ki/Pitch_%28music%29)). A semitone, by
comparison, is 100 cents.

relative-pitch.wrapped_text:
Relative Pitch
Relative pitch is the skill of naming or
singing a note by its interval from a
reference note. It is quite common among
musicians. With it, a singer can read a melody
from a score and pitch each note from the note
before it, and a player of a fretless
instrument can play in tune with others
([Relative pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wik
i/Relative_pitch)).

People also remember the exact pitch of
recordings that they know well, even when they
cannot name the notes:

- Schellenberg and Trehub played 5-second
excerpts of familiar TV theme songs to college
students. Each excerpt was at its original
pitch or moved up or down by 1 or 2 semitones,
and the listeners picked out the original
pitch level. The study concludes that good
pitch memory is widespread among adults with
no music training ([Schellenberg and Trehub 20
03](https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9280.03432)).
- Levitin asked 46 people to sing two popular
songs from memory. Of them, 40% sang the pitch
of the recording in at least one trial, and
44% came within two semitones in both trials
([Levitin
1994](https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03206733)).

absolute-pitch.wrapped_text:
Absolute Pitch
Absolute pitch, often called perfect pitch, is
the skill of naming or singing a note with no
reference note ([Absolute pitch](https://en.wi
kipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_pitch)). Levitin
splits it into two skills: pitch memory, which
is common, and pitch labeling, which is less
common ([Levitin
1994](https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03206733)).

How many people have absolute pitch is not
known exactly. A rate of 1 in 10,000 is widely
reported ([Absolute pitch](https://en.wikipedi
a.org/wiki/Absolute_pitch)). A 2019 review
found a rate of at least 4% among music
students ([Carden and Cline 2019](https://doi.
org/10.1177/0305735619856098)). A test of
music conservatory students in the United
States and China found absolute pitch more
often in students who started music training
earlier. For each starting age, it was far
more common in the Chinese students. They
speak Mandarin, a tone language in which the
pitch of a syllable changes the meaning of a
word ([Deutsch and others
2006](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.2151799)).

pitch-and-color.wrapped_text:
Pitch Compared With Color
Pitch and color share a structure. Hue is an
attribute of color, such as red or blue.
Chroma is the matching attribute of a pitch,
and all pitches with one chroma form one pitch
class, so C3 and C4 share the chroma C ([Pitch
class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_cla
ss)). Chroma repeats every octave, and pitch
height tells which octave a note is in ([Pitch
](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_%28music
%29)).

Naming differs. Almost everyone names colors,
but few people name pitches. Researchers
compare absolute pitch with color naming: most
people learn to name blue from the light they
see, and people who hear notes together with
their names early in life are more likely to
name a C ([Absolute pitch](https://en.wikipedi
a.org/wiki/Absolute_pitch)).

The sense organs differ too:

- The eye has three types of cone cells, so it
reduces the spectrum of any light to three
numbers. Lights with different spectra can
therefore look the same. Such lights are
metamers ([Metamerism](https://en.wikipedia.or
g/wiki/Metamerism_%28color%29)).
- The ear analyzes the spectrum at many places
along the basilar membrane. Two tones that are
further apart than a critical band excite
separate places, so the ear resolves them. Two
tones closer than that interact, and the
listener hears beats or roughness ([Critical b
and](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_ba
nd)).

About the Numbers
The key counts, frequencies, cents and note lengths
in this map come from the Python script below. It
ran with Python 3.12 in November 2026. It uses
twelve-tone equal temperament with A4 at 440 Hz. A
tuned piano has stretched octaves, so its real
frequencies differ from these values, most at the
two ends of the keyboard. The pictures use the same
values.

```python
import math

NAMES = ["A", "A♯/B♭", "B", "C", "C♯/D♭", "D",
"D♯/E♭", "E", "F", "F♯/G♭", "G", "G♯/A♭"]


def key_name(n):
"""Name of piano key n (1 = A0, 88 = C8)."""
octave = (n + 8) // 12
return f"{NAMES[(n - 1) % 12]}{octave}"


def key_freq(n):
"""Frequency of piano key n in Hz, with key 49 (A4)
at 440 Hz."""
return 440 * 2 ** ((n - 49) / 12)


def cents(ratio):
return 1200 * math.log2(ratio)


white = [n for n in range(1, 89) if "♯" not in
key_name(n)]
print("keys:", 88, "white:", len(white), "black:",
88 - len(white))
for n in (1, 40, 49, 88):
print(f"key {n} = {key_name(n)} {key_freq(n):.3f}
Hz")
for n in range(40, 53):
print(f"key {n} {key_name(n)} {key_freq(n):.2f}
Hz")

for h in range(1, 9):
f = 440 * h
n = round(12 * math.log2(f / 440) + 49)
print(f"{h} x 440 = {f} Hz, nearest key
{key_name(n)} {key_freq(n):.2f} Hz, {cents(f /
key_freq(n)):+.1f} cents")

for label, ratio, steps in (("fifth 3:2", 3 / 2,
7), ("fourth 4:3", 4 / 3, 5), ("major third 5:4", 5
/ 4, 4)):
print(f"{label}: {cents(ratio):.2f} cents; {steps}
semitones = {steps * 100} cents")

bpm = 120
for label, beats in (("whole", 4), ("half", 2),
("dotted quarter", 1.5), ("quarter", 1), ("eighth",
0.5)):
print(f"{label}: {beats} beats = {beats * 60 / bpm}
s")
```

- `key 40 = C4 261.626 Hz` and `key 88 = C8
4186.009 Hz`
- `key 41 C♯/D♭4 277.18 Hz`
- `3 x 440 = 1320 Hz, nearest key E6 1318.51 Hz,
+2.0 cents`
- `5 x 440 = 2200 Hz, nearest key C♯/D♭7 2217.46
Hz, -13.7 cents`
- `7 x 440 = 3080 Hz, nearest key G7 3135.96 Hz,
-31.2 cents`
- `fifth 3:2: 701.96 cents; 7 semitones = 700
cents`
- `dotted quarter: 1.5 beats = 0.75 s`
